Subject: Clarifying termination & renewal crediting for 3-year upfront

Hi Markus,

Thanks again for the walkthrough earlier this week. Acme's procurement and finance teams are reviewing the 3-year upfront quote and we hit two substantive questions from tax/treasury that I want to clarify before we move to legal redlines:

1) Early termination refund waterfall — we need an explicit formula in the MSA that ties refunds to remaining committed spend while netting any consumed usage. Finance prefers a schedule that phases the refund over the remaining term (not a single flat percentage) so they can model cash flow.

2) Renewal crediting / co-terming — if we convert unused committed dollars into credits at renewal, we need to understand how credits are applied across new renewals vs. add-on purchases and whether credits retain the original discount level.

Attached is a simple spreadsheet from our side that shows the waterfall they'd accept as a starting point (proposed_refund_matrix.xlsx). Can you confirm Redwood's tolerance on: a) refund timeline (how quickly you return prepaid amounts after termination), b) whether credits keep the original prepay discount, and c) any banking/escrow requirements?

Goal: get buy-in on mechanics so Legal can focus on language rather than negotiating economics.

Best,
Susan Lopez
Head of Procurement
Acme Corp

Attachments: proposed_refund_matrix.xlsx

From: Markus Klein <markus_klein@redwood.com>
To: Susan Lopez <susan.lopez@acmecorp.com>
Date: Sun, 02 May 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Clarifying termination & renewal crediting for 3-year upfront

Hi Susan — thanks for the note and for the clear spreadsheet. High level responses:

• Refund waterfall: Redwood is open to a time-decaying refund schedule tied to remaining prepaid months, with a small operational retention to cover provisioning ramp (we typically propose 2–6% depending on term).
• Refund timing: standard is 30 days after effective termination once usage reconciliation is complete; we can accelerate to 14 business days for larger strategic customers.
• Renewal crediting: credits can be applied to renewals and add-ons, but discounts on credits will depend on whether the customer retains the same committed tier. In practice, credits keep the original USD value (not a percent), and discounting on future purchases is negotiated at renewal.

I'll loop in our pricing and legal counterparts to draft a short economic appendix and a clean term to avoid back-and-forth. 

Sharing a copy of our term sheet with the typical waterfall language as well.

—Markus

Markus — forwarding Susan's spreadsheet and your high-level reply. Quick internal thread to align before we send language to Acme legal. My suggested positions below.

On Sun, May 2, 2027 at 9:12 AM Markus Klein <markus_klein@redwood.com> wrote:

Proposed internal ask / clarifications:
1) Operational retention: for a 3-year prepay at this scale (ACME number in hubspot) I recommend sticking to a 4% retention (covers deprovisioning + short-term GPU allocations). KarThik — can we run a quick model that shows unit economics if we accept 4% vs 2%?
2) Refund phasing: Acme wants phasing; we should offer a monthly pro-rata refund with a cliff after year one (e.g., 100% refund of remaining months * (1 - retention) for year 1–12, 85% for months 13–24, 60% for months 25–36). If legal balks, we can shift to linear decay.
3) Credits & discounting: avoid committing to preserving discount percentages on credits. Commit to USD credit value that applies to renewals/add-ons within 12 months; if they want to extend beyond 12 months, credits convert to a 12-month interest-bearing credit at a small devaluation (e.g., 3% per annum).

Open items: escrow vs Redwood-managed reserve — Acme asked about escrow. Vanessa — do we have a standard escrow playbook for finance?

Thanks,
Lauren
Director, Commercial Finance

From: KarThik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Fwd: Clarifying termination & renewal crediting for 3-year upfront

Thanks — ran two quick scenarios (attached) showing P&L and cash impact for 2% vs 4% retention and the phased refund schedule Lauren proposed. Key takeaways: 

• For ACME-sized deal, 2% retention reduces our immediate cash headroom risk but increases runway exposure if termination spikes. 4% provides a more conservative buffer and keeps economics neutral across reasonable churn assumptions.
• Accelerated refund (14 business days) materially increases processing overhead; recommend 30 days as default but offer 14 days as an SLA-backed option for a premium or for strategic accounts.
• Credits: modeling USD-credit carryforward at face value is simplest for accounting. If credits preserve historic discount %, we create deferred revenue complexities and margin leakage on future seat consumption.

Recommendation: accept Lauren's proposed phasing, set retention at 4% for this tier, default refund timing 30 days with 14 business days as a paid option, and contractually represent credits as USD values valid for 12 months.

- KarThik
Sr. Finance Manager, Revenue Ops

Attachments: retention_pnl_scenarios.xlsx

Markus — appreciate the quick internal alignment. A few follow-ups from Acme finance/legal after reviewing your positions:

1) The phased refund example is acceptable, but legal asked that the MSA include an explicit formula rather than a table. They want the refund amount = (PrepaidRemaining - Retention) * PhaseMultiplier, where PhaseMultiplier is a linear function of months remaining.
2) They want credits to retain the original effective discount for any renewals within 12 months (rather than USD face value). This is a sticking point from our CFO who wants to avoid losing the negotiated discount on future purchases.
3) Escrow: Acme would prefer a short-term escrow for the first 12 months of the prepay to mitigate counterparty risk. If Redwood will not accept escrow, they request a bank guarantee or proof of balance sheet sufficiency.

Can you confirm whether Redwood can: a) accept formula-based language, b) preserve discount on credits for 12 months, c) consider escrow only for the first 12 months (then revert to Redwood-managed reserve)?

Thanks — Susan

From: Markus Klein <markus_klein@redwood.com>
To: Susan Lopez <susan.lopez@acmecorp.com>
Cc: Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.com>, KarThik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>, Vanessa Ortiz <vanessa_ortiz@redwood.com>
Date: Thu, 06 May 2027 09:22:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Clarifying termination & renewal crediting for 3-year upfront

Susan — thanks for the clear asks. Confirming Redwood's positions so legal has concrete inputs: 

1) Formula: yes — we can accept a formulaic definition of refund that references remaining prepaid USD and a PhaseMultiplier. We'll propose exact math that mirrors the phased table (linear decay by month with an initial operational retention). Draft clause will read: Refund = (RemainingPrepaidUSD * (1 - RetentionPercent)) * PhaseMultiplier(MonthsRemaining) where PhaseMultiplier = max(0, (MonthsRemaining / TotalMonths)^(1)) with negotiated breakpoints at 24 and 12 months (we will include explicit multipliers to match the phased schedule).

2) Credits / discounting: we cannot commit to preserving historical discount percentages on credits across all future commercial scenarios; doing so creates deferred revenue and margin unpredictability. That said, we will accept preserving the effective economic value for renewals that execute within 90 days of termination (i.e., credits applied to a renewal executed inside 90 days will maintain discount parity). For renewals beyond 90 days but within 12 months, credits will apply at face USD value; Redwood will give a good-faith price-protection conversation but cannot legally lock in percentage discounts beyond 90 days.

3) Escrow: Redwood prefers not to hold funds in third-party escrow because it limits our ability to allocate capacity and causes settlement friction. We will accept a limited escrow for the first 6 months of the prepay for a nominal fee and provide a bank guarantee for the remainder of year one if Acme requires additional credit support. After 12 months we revert to Redwood-managed reserve. If Acme agrees, legal can draft a short escrow addendum.

Next steps: if these positions are acceptable in principle, I'll ask legal to draft the economic appendix and a short escrow addendum for review. Happy to jump on a call Friday to close.

—Markus
Head of Sales, Enterprise
Redwood Inference
